approved: Crimes Legislation Amendment (Psychoactive Substances and Other Measures) Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would ban importing substances that mimic illegal drugs but are not yet controlled, and substances presented as alternatives to illegal drugs.
Customs officers could search for, detain, seize and destroy these banned substances without a warrant, using powers similar to those for other prohibited goods.
A defendant charged with importing a banned substance would have to prove the substance is exempt, shifting the evidential burden to them.
Creates new offences for importing prohibited psychoactive substances and prohibited serious drug alternatives.
Gives Customs officers warrantless search, seizure and destruction powers for these substances.
Places an evidential burden on defendants to show their imported substance is exempt.
Importers of psychoactive substances and serious drug alternatives, and Australian Customs and Border Protection Service officers.

Jan McLucas by leave—I move opposition amendments (1) and (2) on sheet 7657 together: (1) Schedule 2, item 14, page 16 (lines 17 to 24), to be opposed. (2) Schedule 2, item 18, page 21 (lines 13 to 18), section 361.5 to be opposed. These amendments oppose mandatory minimum sentences for the reasons that Senator Collins outlined during the second reading debate. Richard Colbeck The government does not support these amendments. Firearms trafficking is amongst the most serious of crimes, particularly given its ability to facilitate violent and potentially deadly criminal acts. The entry of even a small number of illegal firearms into the Australian community will have a significant impact on the threat posed by the illicit market and due to the enduring nature of firearms a firearm can remain within that market for many years. Mandatory minimum penalties send a very strong message on the seriousness of gun related crime and violence and certainly act as a deterrent for criminals. The government believes that mandatory minimum sentences are a stronger deterrent than increased maximum penalties. There are protections in place to ensure that mandatory minimums do not cause unjust results. Mandatory minimum sentences will not apply to children, and there is no minimum non-parole period. The offences preserve a level of judicial discretion to allow courts to take into account mitigating factors when setting the period offenders spend in custody. The government amended the explanatory memorandum in response to the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee's report to make clear that mandatory minimum sentence is not intended as a guide to the non-parole period, which in some cases may result in significant differences between the head sentence and the non-parole period. Supported the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Psychoactive Substances and Other Measures) Bill 2014, which bans the importation of unregulated new psychoactive substances, expands firearms trafficking offences, and streamlines the international transfer of prisoners scheme, but flagged Labor's concerns about a new mandatory minimum five-year prison term for firearms offences.

Supported the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Psychoactive Substances and Other Measures) Bill 2014 to ban new psychoactive substances not yet regulated, described drug and alcohol harms in Geraldton in the Durack electorate, and noted that White Ribbon Day, marking one woman a week dying from domestic violence in Australia, fell the next day.

Said Labor supported the bill's psychoactive substances measures but opposed its mandatory minimum sentencing provisions for firearms trafficking, citing Law Council concerns, and noted crystal methamphetamine use among injecting drug users had risen 39 per cent between 2010 and 2011, with more than 20,000 methamphetamine related medical episodes recorded nationally between 2012 and 2013.

Supported the bill, citing UK data showing deaths linked to new psychoactive substances rising from six in 2003 to 52 in 2012, and noting New South Wales banned synthetic drugs in 2013 after the death of Sydney student Henry Kwan, while also referencing the removal of 700,000 firearms following the 1996 Port Arthur reforms.

Commended the bill, noting firearms were used in 25 per cent of homicides in Australia in 2012, and highlighted new mandatory minimum sentences of five years for firearms trafficking and an $88 million commitment to Customs and Border Protection to increase cargo screening.

As a former criminal lawyer, supported the omnibus bill's five schedules covering new psychoactive substances, firearms trafficking, international prisoner transfers and slavery jurisdiction, and welcomed mandatory minimum five year sentences for firearms trafficking offences.

Supported the bill, citing an estimated $600 million legal market for new psychoactive substances in 2012, and noting five deaths, including three school children, in Victoria over 14 months, while also welcoming tougher firearms penalties given firearms are used in 25 per cent of Australian homicides.

Supported the bill, noting the electorate of more than 145,000 people includes a high proportion of 15 to 24 year olds, and cited Europol data showing 280 new psychoactive substances under monitoring and UK deaths linked to them rising from six in 2003 to 52 in 2013.
Opened remarks on the bill by thanking the Deputy Speaker for coming in to hear the speech.

Supported the bill, citing the deaths of two New South Wales teenagers from the drug NBOMe in 2012 and 2013, and Australian Crime Commission data showing 250,000 illicit long arms in circulation in 2012, with firearms used in at least 113 of that year's murders.

Concluded the debate by praising Queensland's Safe Night Out strategy and its section 4C amendment to the Drugs Misuse Act 1986 as a model, noting 348 new psychoactive substances had been reported globally and that products mimicking cannabis alone had doubled from 60 to 110 between 2012 and 2013.

Argued that the bill would target new psychoactive substances, strengthen firearms-trafficking penalties, modernise prisoner transfers, provide universal jurisdiction over slavery offences, and improve anti-money-laundering measures, while retaining sentencing discretion by excluding people under 18 and not imposing a non-parole period.

Moved amendments to exclude plants, fungi and their extracts from the psychoactive-substances import ban and to extend financial-intelligence access to Victoria's Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission and Queensland's Crime and Corruption Commission, while clarifying tax-information disclosures and related explanatory material.

Argued that Labor's Senate amendments strengthened the government's firearms smuggling bill, which he said was based on the previous Labor government's own legislation, and opposed the government's mandatory minimum sentencing addition as contrary to the Attorney-General's Department's own guidance against minimum penalties.
